claims.text: Standard alloying and conventional processing typically produce homogeneous, often single-phase, or otherwise non-optimized dual-phase HEA microstructures.
Integrated atomistic-to-mesoscale models can identify thermomechanical processing parameters that generate the desired local order and phase structure.
Controlled deformation followed by rapid annealing can induce deformation-driven local chemical ordering.
The proposed thermomechanical treatment can promote formation of a dual-phase microstructure.
The target dual-phase structure consists of a metastable phase embedded in a stable matrix and is coupled to dynamic local chemical order.
Dynamic local chemical order can develop during deformation and prior thermomechanical processing in FCC entropy alloys.
Heat treatment can alter local or short-range chemical order in CoCrNi-type alloys.
Local chemical ordering can increase strength and work hardening, thereby contributing to a favorable strength-ductility combination.
The local-order and dual-phase microstructure decouples the intrinsic trade-off between strength and ductility.
Composite-like deformation mechanisms arising from the dual-phase microstructure improve mechanical performance.
Phase-boundary constraints in the dual-phase microstructure increase Young's modulus.
The dual-phase microstructure improves fracture resistance through crack deflection and crack arrest.
The computationally guided treatment will simultaneously improve strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance relative to conventional processing.
Each of the four targeted properties may improve by approximately 10–20%.
The intervention should work at ambient and service-relevant mechanical testing conditions.
The intervention requires an HEA composition with sufficient chemical complexity and suitable elemental interactions to support dynamic ordering and dual-phase behavior.
Processing outside the computationally predicted parameter window may fail to produce the target microstructure.
Service-induced microstructural coarsening can eliminate the fine-scale features and negate their mechanical benefits.
Atom probe tomography can be used to detect and quantify local or short-range chemical order after processing.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant improvement greater than 5% in all four properties, or failure to form the predicted microstructure, is defined as falsification.
